article_title: Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah
citation: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://web.stanford.edu/~mshanks/MichaelShanks/files/509554.pdf
title: Dear Colleague Letter crosswalk of federal recommendations and R15CC considerations for resource equity provisions
description: Table 1 of the report is a crosswalk pairing the U.S. Department of Education's July 2023 Dear Colleague Letter recommendations (A.1 through A.9 on state resource allocation reviews and B.1 through B.4 on CSI and ATSI plans) with R15CC considerations drawn from the Utah technical assistance. The report explains that "The accompanying crosswalk (Table 1) includes the Department's recommendations, including considerations based on the technical assistance R15CC provided while designing the RAR from 2020 to 2023." Each row adds guiding questions for states on topics such as defining significant numbers of identified schools, defining financial and nonfinancial resources, aligning review timing, integrating with monitoring and budgeting, comparing allocation data, disaggregating by student group, stakeholder engagement, feedback, public posting, and plan templates and guidance.
requirements: States should use the crosswalk to align their RAR design with the Department's nonregulatory guidance on Title I, Part A resource equity provisions.
constraints: The crosswalk addresses the two referenced resource equity provisions: the state resource allocation review requirement and identifying and addressing resource inequities in CSI and ATSI plans.
target_learning_goals: implementing ESSA resource equity provisions through resource allocation reviews
examples: Example considerations include organizing LEAs and schools into cohorts so review timing is meaningful and sustainable, and beginning with existing data in the state's accountability systems when analyzing equity.
key_sources: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://web.stanford.edu/~mshanks/MichaelShanks/files/509554.pdf

citation: Clark, J.M., Paivio, A. Dual coding theory and education. Educ Psychol Rev 3, 149–210 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01320076
title: Use DCT's concrete models of student, teacher, and educational psychologist behavior to strengthen pedagogical practice
description: The article recommends grounding pedagogical practice in the concrete models that dual coding theory offers for the behavior and experience of educational participants. It argues that "the concrete models that DCT offers for the behavior and experience of students, teachers, and educational psychologists further our understanding of educational phenomena and strengthen related pedagogical practices." The principle treats DCT-based modeling as a route to improved educational design and understanding.
requirements: Practitioners and researchers must adopt DCT's concrete models of the behavior and experience of students, teachers, and educational psychologists
constraints: The article states that much additional research needs to be done
target_learning_goals: understanding of educational phenomena
strengthening pedagogical practices
examples: The article shows how basic DCT mechanisms model diverse educational phenomena including learning and memory of school material and effective instruction
key_sources: Clark, J.M., Paivio, A. Dual coding theory and education. Educ Psychol Rev 3, 149–210 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01320076

article_title: <p>Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation</p>
citation: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514
title: Standardized assessment tools for DCD and dysgraphia diagnosis (MABC-2, TGMD-2, DCDQ, BHK, Minnesota Handwriting Assessment, ETCH)
description: The review catalogs the standardized instruments used to diagnose DCD and dysgraphia. The MABC-2, the most widely used DCD tool, consists of 8 items across three age ranges (3–6, 7–10, 11–16 years), lasts 40–50 mins, and covers manual dexterity, ball skills, and balance. The TGMD-2 is a norm-referenced measure of gross motor skills with 2 subtests probing 12 skills for children aged 3–10–11 years, lasting 15–20 mins. The DCDQ is a brief parental screening questionnaire for children aged 5–15 years. For dysgraphia, the BHK (standardized on 837 children aged 6–11) yields legibility and speed scores, alongside the Minnesota Handwriting Assessment and the ETCH.
requirements: Guidelines for administration must be followed to ensure reliability of standardized psychomotor batteries and scales
constraints: Unlike DCD, there is no gold standard for diagnosing dysgraphia, probably because writing systems differ substantially between countries and languages
target_learners: Children with suspected dysgraphia in Grades 1–6
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing motor coordination and handwriting difficulties and establishing baselines for intervention
examples: The BHK requires participants to copy a text for 5 mins on an unlined sheet, scored on 13 legibility criteria plus writing speed
key_sources: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514

article_title: Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design
citation: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y
title: Divergent Collaborative Learning Mechanisms (DCLM) framework for coding collaboration with divergent goals
description: The editorial describes Tissenbaum, Berland, and Lyons' framework "for recognizing and coding collaboration and divergent learning — Divergent Collaborative Learning Mechanisms (DCLM)", used to analyze museum visitors' interactions with an interactive digital tabletop exhibit. It challenges the assumption that productive collaboration requires shared objectives, showing collaborative learning occurred among visitors "while holding divergent conceptions and pursuing divergent goals."
requirements: A designed tabletop exhibit supporting loosely-coupled interactions so visitors can explore independently while observing and interacting with others
constraints: The framework was applied in a museum setting with naturalistic visitor groups; the editorial notes relatively few tabletop studies had a clear CSCL theoretical stance
target_learners: museum visitors in informal learning settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning under divergent goals, e.g., about electric circuits
examples: Interaction analysis was used to analyze joint effort among visitors interacting with a tabletop exhibit supporting loosely-coupled exploration
key_sources: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y

article_title: Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology
citation: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6
title: Integration of dimensional comparisons into situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT): relativistic expectancy and value formation across domains
description: Eccles and Wigfield (2020) developed SEVT to explain individual differences in expectancies, values, and their consequences for achievement and choices; Wigfield et al. (2020) presented the connection of DCT with SEVT in detail. The review explains that this extension affords a more relativistic reading, where "the question being asked is less "Can I do X?" and more "How well can I do X compared to Y?," less "Do I want to do X?" and more "Do I want to do X more than Y?"." All facets playing a role in SEVT can also be predictors, moderators, and criteria in dimensional comparisons, underpinning that dimensional comparisons impact the formation of both expectancy and subjective task values.
requirements: Subjective task values are heterogeneous in domain-specificity, so they should be influenced to different extents by dimensional comparisons
constraints: The review notes costs, which differ strongly between domains, should be more strongly determined by dimensional contrast effects than utility values, which vary less strongly between subjects
target_learning_goals: expectancy formation
subjective task value formation
academic choice
examples: Wigfield et al. (2020) presented in detail the connection of DCT with SEVT in a separate theoretical paper
key_sources: Jens Möller. (2024). Ten Years of Dimensional Comparison Theory: On the Development of a Theory from Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09918-6

article_title: Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized, Controlled Trial
citation: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335
title: Developing Collaboration and Consultation Skills (DCCS) professional development program model
description: The DCCS program is a teacher professional development model combining a five-day summer institute, four follow-up application modules, in-school instructional coaching about every six weeks, and weekly 30-minute collaboration between ESL and classroom teachers. It is designed to close what the authors call the "implementation gap" by building teachers' high-impact instructional strategies for English learners, a collaboration framework, and incorporation of families' cultural wealth. The design intentionally builds on scaffolding, the gradual release of responsibility, and learning by doing.
requirements: School-based teams of ESL and classroom teachers must collaborate for 30 minutes each week
Ongoing support mechanisms such as coaching and follow-up modules must accompany the initial institute
constraints: The pilot was conducted with 45 teachers and 105 students in 12 elementary schools, so evidence of effectiveness is preliminary pending a larger trial
target_learners: Young Latino English learners in kindergarten through second grade
target_learning_goals: English language and literacy development
Academic content learning
examples: Teachers attended 35 hours of professional development during the Summer Institute and an additional 6 hours during the modules, with coaching during structured collaboration meetings
key_sources: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. article_title: Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized, Controlled Trial
citation: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335
title: DCCS collaboration framework: working alliance plus time, structure, and accountability
description: The collaboration framework introduced in the DCCS program consists of two critical components: a working alliance, which addresses process characteristics such as effective communication, positive regard, and reciprocal leadership, and time, structure, and accountability (TSA), which covers time management, group norms and roles, and accountability measures. Teachers use it in weekly meetings to align content and language objectives, plan strategy implementation across ESL and regular classrooms, and review the previous week's plan. The model allows flexibility in teachers' choice of strategies to promote sustained use after developer support ends.
requirements: Weekly structured collaboration meetings between ESL and classroom teachers
Explicit description of roles and group norms
constraints: Most teachers have not had preparation in how to work collaboratively with colleagues, per the article's background
target_learners: ESL teachers and classroom teachers of English learners in elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Aligning language and content instruction for English learners across classroom settings
examples: One ESL teacher planned to teach vocabulary from an upcoming science lesson, and both teachers planned to use sentence frames to support oral language with the new vocabulary
key_sources: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. article_title: Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized, Controlled Trial
citation: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). Improving Young English Learners' Language and Literacy Skills Through Teacher Professional Development: A Randomized Controlled Trial. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217732335
title: DCCS instructional strategies organized by constrained versus unconstrained literacy skills
description: The DCCS program teaches a set of nine instructional strategies organized by whether they target constrained skills, which students can master over a relatively short time (Say It Move It, Blend as You Go, Word Card for phonemic awareness, phonics, and word recognition), or unconstrained skills, which continue to develop across time (Teaching Cognates, Vocabulary Text Talk, Frayer Model, Modified DRA, and oral and written Sentence Frames for vocabulary and comprehension). The program addresses both but provides much greater emphasis on unconstrained skills such as vocabulary and comprehension, based on persistent reading comprehension gaps for English learners.
requirements: Teachers need PD training and practice in each strategy, progressing from simpler word recognition strategies to more complex vocabulary and comprehension strategies
constraints: The five key literacy domains are necessary for English learners but not sufficient; sensitive modulation of instruction and a focus on English language development are also vital, per August and Shanahan as cited by the article
target_learners: Kindergarten through second grade Latino English learners
target_learning_goals: Phonemic awareness, phonics, vocabulary, comprehension, and oral language development
examples: Teachers used a modified Directed Reading Activity followed by language frames to support students' summarizing of texts, and frequently used the Vocabulary Text Talk strategy
key_sources: Leslie M. Babinski, Steven J. Amendum, Steven E. Knotek, Marta Sánchez, Patrick Malone. (2018). article_title: The Effect of Explicit Metapragmatic Instruction on Request Speech Act Awareness of Intermediate EFL Students at Institute Level
citation: Fatemeh Abdollahizadeh Masouleh, Masoumeh Arjmandi, Fereydoon Vahdany. (2014). The Effect of Explicit Metapragmatic Instruction on Request Speech Act Awareness of Intermediate EFL Students at Institute Level. Universal Journal of Educational Research 2(7): 504-511. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2014.020702
title: 20-situation Discourse Completion Test for request speech act awareness
description: The study's measure was a written Discourse Completion Test questionnaire developed by Jalilifar (2009), consisting of "20 situations followed by a blank space in which the participants were asked to write a request accordingly". Items were chosen for relevance to a university student's life so learners could imagine the scenarios. Each correct item was awarded one mark, with a maximum score of 20, and the same questionnaire served as pretest and posttest.
requirements: Situations relevant to the learners' life context so they can imagine the scenarios
Written form so learners can reply without language difficulties
constraints: Measures written request production on a 20-point scale; the article reports test-retest administration at term start and end for reliability
target_learning_goals: request speech act realization and awareness
examples: Appendix A prints the 20 scenarios, including asking a stranger for a photo, requesting an assignment extension, and asking a professor to reschedule a test

article_title: Investigating the Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Shima Rajabi, Akbar Azizifar, & Habib Gowhary. (2015). Investigating the of Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.53
title: Discourse Completion Test (DCT) for assessing apology speech act appropriateness
description: The study used a Discourse Completion Test as its pre- and post-test measure. The DCT is described as "a kind of questionnaire which contains series of concisely defined situations used to elicit special speech acts". The pre-test consisted of four apology scenarios varying social status and social distance, and the post-test comprised 12 situations. Responses were scored on a five-point analytic Likert appropriateness scale following Farahian, Rezaee and Gholami (2012), where "scale of 5 indicates 'completely appropriate'".
requirements: Situations selected to vary social status and social distance variables
constraints: DCT elicits written rather than spoken production; the article notes it is used at the early stage of learning communicative functions
target_learners: Iranian EFL learners at intermediate and advanced levels
target_learning_goals: Appropriate use of apology strategies
examples: Pre-test scenarios included returning rain-damaged borrowed notes and spilling tea on a staff member's desk; post-test scenarios included forgetting a meeting with a boss
key_sources: Shima Rajabi, Akbar Azizifar, & Habib Gowhary. (2015). Investigating the of Explicit Instruction of Apology Speech Act on Pragmatic Development of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.4p.53

article_title: The Effect of Teaching Interlanguage Pragmatics on Interpretation Ability of Iranian Translation Students
citation: Mahnaz Mahmoudi Ravesh, Hossein Heidari Tabrizi. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Interlanguage Pragmatics on Interpretation Ability of Iranian Translation Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 8(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.3p.44
title: Discourse Completion Test for measuring interlanguage pragmatics
description: A Discourse Completion Test (DCT) is a written questionnaire consisting of designed situations used to elicit specific speech acts, each containing a prompt to make it easy for participants to respond in writing. The study used a DCT adapted from Blum-Kulka (1980) to measure participants' initial interlanguage pragmatic knowledge prior to ILP instruction, chosen because DCTs are easy to use and provide rich data in a comparably short period of time.
requirements: Situations must embed status levels so participants know which strategy to use when status differs, whether being lower, equal, or higher
constraints: The article notes, citing Cummings (2006), that DCTs are incapable of depicting real-life interaction
target_learners: EFL learners of diverse cultural backgrounds
target_learning_goals: interlanguage pragmatic knowledge of speech acts
examples: The DCT used in this study was adapted from Blum-Kulka (1980) and its purpose was to examine interlanguage knowledge
key_sources: Mahnaz Mahmoudi Ravesh, Hossein Heidari Tabrizi. (2017). The Effect of Teaching Interlanguage Pragmatics on Interpretation Ability of Iranian Translation Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 8(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.8n.3p.44

article_title: The dynamic case-based learning model: conducive to enhancing the practical learning effectiveness of dermatology for medical students.
citation: Li Yidan, Lei Li, Jiang Ling, Mao Ping, Fu Chuhan, Chen Jing, Zeng Qinghai. (2025). The dynamic case-based learning model: conducive to enhancing the practical learning effectiveness of dermatology for medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07474-3
title: Dynamic case-based learning (DCBL) model
description: The DCBL model embeds the temporal dimension of disease progression into case-based teaching for dermatology practical education. Cases are arranged chronologically so that "Educators continuously monitor patient conditions to update the clinical database, while students use lesion images and disease records to engage in dynamic observation and analysis", refining diagnoses and treatment plans in real time. It is grounded in Social Constructivist theory and Situated Learning Theory, positioning students to co-construct understanding through interaction and authentic context-rich experiences, moving from rote learning toward diagnostic reasoning and adaptive clinical problem-solving.
requirements: Typical dynamic cases with chronological clinical images, auxiliary examination results, and treatment plans at each time point of disease progression
Educators who continuously monitor patient conditions and update the clinical database
constraints: The article reports the model had not yet been implemented in actual teaching at the time of the study; effectiveness evidence is limited to perceptions
target_learning_goals: dynamic understanding of skin lesion progression
diagnostic and therapeutic clinical reasoning
self-directed learning
examples: Cases of 11 commonly occurring skin disease categories were compiled into structured PowerPoint presentations illustrating lesion evolution over time
key_sources: Li Yidan, Lei Li, Jiang Ling, Mao Ping, Fu Chuhan, Chen Jing, Zeng Qinghai. (2025). The dynamic case-based learning model: conducive to enhancing the practical learning effectiveness of dermatology for medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07474-3

article_title: The dynamic case-based learning model: conducive to enhancing the practical learning effectiveness of dermatology for medical students.
citation: Li Yidan, Lei Li, Jiang Ling, Mao Ping, Fu Chuhan, Chen Jing, Zeng Qinghai. (2025). The dynamic case-based learning model: conducive to enhancing the practical learning effectiveness of dermatology for medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07474-3
title: Dynamic case database and structured PowerPoint presentations for dermatology
description: The article's core instructional artifact is a collection of typical dynamic cases transformed into structured PowerPoint presentations. The authors "collected typical cases of 11 clinically commonly occurring skin diseases", arranging clinical images, auxiliary examination results, and treatment plans chronologically for each time point of disease progression, supplemented by patient demographics, histories, and laboratory reports. Case selection criteria included typical dynamic manifestations, high clinical relevance, differential-diagnosis value, and sufficient auxiliary examination data.
requirements: Informed consent from patients for clinical data and image collection
Cases accompanied by sufficient auxiliary examination results and imaging data
constraints: Using PowerPoint presentations as a simulation tool may lead to varying interpretations of the DCBL model among respondents, per the article's limitations section
target_learning_goals: recognizing skin lesion morphology and its dynamic progression
integrating clinical manifestations with diagnostic findings
examples: A schematic diagram of dynamic case data illustrates a typical case with images and treatment plans ordered chronologically (Fig. 1)
key_sources: Li Yidan, Lei Li, Jiang Ling, Mao Ping, Fu Chuhan, Chen Jing, Zeng Qinghai. (2025). The dynamic case-based learning model: conducive to enhancing the practical learning effectiveness of dermatology for medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07474-3

article_title: Medical school department chair performance improvement: A qualitative study.
citation: Mahboubi M, Ahmady S, Mirzazadeh A, Zarei A, Hamidi H, Kohan N. (2024). Medical school department chair performance improvement: A qualitative study. PLoS One 19(3): e0294927. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294927
title: Five-theme conceptual framework of factors influencing medical school department chair performance improvement
description: The article develops a schematic conceptual framework (Fig 1) from thematic analysis of focus groups with deans and department chairs at Iranian medical schools. It organizes the factors into five overarching themes: "1) Job preparation and expectations factors, 2) organizational behaviour management factors, 3) performance support system, 4) leadership and 5) financial resources development", with nine themes and thirty-two sub-themes. The framework holds that higher managers help chairs through communication, motivation and culture, while chairs need support systems, leadership development and financial resources.
requirements: Clarifying expectations and job descriptions before evaluation and audit using anticipated indicators
constraints: Findings derive from a qualitative, context-centered Iranian medical education setting, which the authors say makes generalizability across contexts difficult
target_learning_goals: Improve department chair performance in leading academic departments
Develop leadership and management capability of academic leaders
examples: Two focus group discussion sessions of around 90 minutes each with 20 purposefully sampled deans and chairs, analyzed via Braun and Clarke thematic analysis with member checking
key_sources: Mahboubi M, Ahmady S, Mirzazadeh A, Zarei A, Hamidi H, Kohan N. (2024). Medical school department chair performance improvement: A qualitative study. PLoS One 19(3): e0294927. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0294927
